newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada court rejects religious-school challenge.
newsitem.headline: Canada court rejects religious-school challenge.

text.p: Canada's Supreme Court on Thursday rejected a demand by minority religious groups for the same public funding for their schools as is given to Roman Catholic schools.

Jewish and conservative Protestant parents in Ontario argued the province unconstitutionally violated their religious freedom and their right to equality by funding Catholic and public schools but not their education.
But the court decided the constitution under which Canada was formed in 1867 guaranteed funding for Catholic schools but not for any other religious groups in Ontario.
Justice Frank Iacobucci, writing for the majority, agreed he constitution "entrenches certain rights with respect to the public funding of religious education.
"However these rights are limited to those which were enjoyed at the time of Confederation (in 1867)."

The majority was 8-1 on the issue of funding of other religious schools. And by 7-2 the court ruled the province did not have to provide health and other services to students in those schools -- for example handicapped students.

"In Ontario all are equal but some are more equal than others," said Moshe Ronen of the Canadian Jewish Congress, which began the challenge in 1990 with the Ontario Alliance of Christian Schools (OACS).

"Parents choosing religious-based schools for their children pay for secular public education through their taxes, and bear the entire cost of their own children's schooling -- discrimination on the basis of religion," OACS President Gerry Steggerda said after the decision.
OACS spokesman John Vanasselt said the court did not bar provinces from choosing to fund other religious schools -- just that they could not be forced to do so.
One of the parents on whose behalf the groups fought was Susie Adler, who said she was paying $14,000 Canadian ($10,500 U.S.) a year to send her son and daughter to a Jewish school.

Farmer Leo Elgersma was another parent, who pays $7,000 ($5,200 U.S.) to send his wheelchair-bound son Walter to a Christian school and who lost government transport and therapy for him when he switched out of the public system.
"Why should I have to pay taxes for one school and pay for my other school by myself? It's very hard for a lot of people," he told Reuters.

A court decision in favour of the parents would have had an impact across Canada and would have been noticed in the United States where many Republicans pushed for the use of tuition vouchers to enable funding of students in private schools.
Other provinces, as well as the Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA), joined Ontario in arguing public schools promoted social unity.
"If they had won the public schools would have been considerably weakened in their ability to play an integrating role," CCLA General Counsel Alan Borovoy said.
